game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game starts very simply:
There was a terror attack, and it’s up to you to investigate all available sources to discover who is responsible.
Basically detective work in the 21st century.
But as the game progresses, you discover there is much more than meets the eye.
Not only the suspects you track, their actions and relationships, but also your actions, and those of your superiors, all become important.
You start off as a mere spectator, but even by witnessing the events, you are already impacting them.
And once you realize your impact on the world you were meant to observe, you’re now faced with difficult choices.
Choices that are not right or wrong - only choices you need live with for the rest of your life…

This is a really good game, that dives deep into questions of terror, accountability, privacy, and more.

The only issue I had with this game, is that even though you don’t have to submit every single piece of evidence you find.
And can be even reprimanded for submitting irrelevant evidence,
The game simply refuses to progress until you submit almost every piece.
For example:
Let’s say you discover a person likes strawberry ice cream. But that has nothing to do with determining if he’s a terrorist or not, so you ignore this piece of info (mark it as ignored).
Then nothing happens. The game simply refuses to progress any further.
So you submit the only remaining piece of info, that the suspect likes strawberry ice cream, and like clockwork, you’re immediately reprimanded by your superior that this piece of data has nothing to do with the case at hand (daaa….).
But then suddenly the suspect receives an incriminating phone call - and the game suddenly starts progressing.

So instead of submitting useless data being a trigger to game progression, simply marking the data as “ignored” should serve the same purpose.

Other than that - it’s a really good game.
Much better than it’s sequel (Ignorance is Strength)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Duration: Just under 5 hours. 

Orwell is a very unique game.  The player takes the persona of an investigator in a futuristic 1984-style society and tries to find information/evidence regarding some terrorist bombings.  There are 5 chapters in the game which take you on a journey.  The first chapter you are closely led by your examiner, but then more and more choices are laid before you as you delve into websites, eavesdrop on phone calls and investigate hard drives.  

The game is somewhat linear and the main choice is to choose if information is relevant or not to the case and avoiding taking things out of context.  For once you claim something is true, it is stuck in stone.  

Overall, playing Orwell (after the first 60 minutes) became a highly engrossing experience.  The delivery is very well done and even builds to a massive tension where getting information at one point is almost frantic as you are listening to a phone call.  I won't give the details away, but it was tense and somewhat chilling conclusion.  

Overall, a very unique game, full of reading text, but well-delivered. 

7/10 Recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The true strength of Orwell lies not in replayability, or even in a strong gameplay mechanic, but in a consuming immersion that relays a story illustrating how powerful a government powered by surveillance could truly be.  You "live" what it would really mean to the lives of people you begin to learn more and about as you coldly monitor them in what feels like real time. 

Unlike other games employing immersive story driven simulations on rails, like "This is the Police" or Uplink, I never once sought to find a "right" solution online.  I accepted that my data was only as good as the research I could see in front of me, and I made some calls based on the psychology of the subjects I digitally (legally) stalked, for the good of The Nation.  By the middle of the game, I couldn't really stop.  It was like binging Netflix, and although pulling back I can clearly see that the game is often holding your hand and guiding you towards the next arc, in the moment the progression feels so natural that I was just excited to unravel the next thread. I performed my role in the Orwell program compliantly. 

The music and the Minority Report style slick UI (that felt so good to work in), combined with the friendly banter of your friendly government advisor led me to the worst part about this game - I started it at 11pm.  I had work at 8am the next day, which only allowed a couple hours of sleep after finally beating the game over 6 straight hours.  

There are unique endings, and the game will bend based on your choices and how far you dig.  When investigating, you don't have to read deeply into every article - Orwell finds the pertinent data for you so you're not forced to muddle through what turns into a mountain of documentation.  Sometimes though, you really need to step back and figure out your suspects murder mystery style, except you do it by going through their files, emails, phone call transcripts, timelines, and chat logs - tying that in with publically available resources. 

And maybe that's the biggest lesson of the game, and of 1984 when you apply a technical layer - in a society where we are constantly generating documents and digital paper trails, you could really learn all you need to know to paint us as however you'd like with the right tools.  It's one thing to read it, but the game lets you feel it. All at once it was exciting, and chilling.

In the end, without offering spoilers, the game never forces you to choose if this is right or wrong.

The total time to beat the game, for me, was 5 hours, but hardly any of that was spent idle. For $10 (I got this on sale at $6), if you have even half the experience I did, the game proves its value quickly.  While you can only replay the game the same way you would reread a book (altered maybe slightly), it did give me a short story worth thinking about for much longer than the gameplay itself lasted.


Pros:

- Immersive gameplay and story
- Great soundtrack
- UI feels fantastic
- Great value
- Story ending felt wrapped up, not abrupt

Cons:

- Limited replayability
- 5 hours of content (I take the time to read a lot of the docs)
- Not super challenging to an average player

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.
Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember.
 
[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
 
Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. However, at times the story does slow down, and it is easy to get fatigued with the sheer amount of writing in this game.
I think it’s easiest to sum up Orwell as an interactive, dystopian, detective novel at its best. In a game that hinges on the “choices matter” idea, it does well in treating the player like an intelligent and competent participant. You have the ability to make inferences that might not accomplish what you’re trying to do. Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching.
 
[h1]8/10[/h1]

The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability. The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control. Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember. [h1]The Verdict[/h1] Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. Orwell is one of those games that makes you think. It makes you think about how surveillance works in the real world. It makes you think about what you put online as this can be misunderstood or taken out of context. It makes you think about what your credit card statement says about you. Most of all though it makes you think about what is considered as right and wrong.

Orwell is a game where you play a person sat at a computer terminal extracting information from the internet about people to stop a series of terrorist bombings. Through what information you decide to pass on to your handler and which conflicting statements you believe the game will pan out very differently. How relevant is it that somebody doesn’t like to go out and party? Not very much on the surface, but what if they later say they are going out clubbing all night? Seems unusual for somebody who actively dislikes this, doesn’t it? Are you reading too much into this? Or is this information going to stop a bombing? Orwell constantly asks you to reassess your understanding of the characters you are investigating. One phone call or chat message could convince you that they are a terrorist or vice versa and you need to just weather the consequences.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
9/10

Orwell is a surveillance game (I suppose you could call it). However, there is also a machine/program in the game called Orwell that gameplay centers around. 

The program seems to have two functions. The first is a tracking function: if the player provides a website, a chat handle, a phone number, an e-mail address, or even a computer ID (I suppose this is analogous to an IP address), the program will then "track" it. If a phone call comes in on the number, you can listen in. If a blog has an update, Orwell lets you know, etc. Often, you'll get a chat handle, then in the chat you'll find a phone number or e-mail, which you can then track. From all this data you can create profiles of persons of interest, which is the second function of the program. Through data, you can learn who knows who, and how they know each other.

Law Enforcement uses the information collected to locate and arrest those individuals that you've deemed possible suspects in crimes. The game begins with a bomb exploding in a public square. I won't give any more of the story away, because it's quite an interesting ride.

On the surface, this gameplay sounds straightforward, but there are juicy complications. For instance, if someone denounces the government harshly in a fit of rage after paying taxes, do they represent a danger to the government? If Orwell (the program) didn't have a human operator, could it read between the lines? To further increase the stakes, any data uploaded to Orwell is permanent. So I couldn't designate this hypothetical taxpayer as a threat and then clarify later that he didn't "mean" what he said.

Also, if someone was aware of the program, could they provide false meeting places to divert law enforcment? Do your persons of interest know that you know they know about Orwell? 

It's a very well done and thought-provoking game, especially in the age of big data. Not only does it explore some of the limitations of using data collection for crime prevention, but it makes the player realize just how much information about themselves they've made public online.

For instance, Judith Duportail (a writer for the Guardian) requested the data that the dating site Tinder had collected on her. In September 2017, she published an article detailing the experience. Tinder sent her 800 pages of material.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm surprised how lukewarm a lot of the reviews of this game are - I thought it was phenomenal! I guess it's because the game is mostly reading?

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time. 

I was super gripped the whole way through and am excited to play the sequel now!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.

I liked this! But it's not without its issues. If I could give a neutral rating I would, but for now it's not bad enough for me to not recommend giving it a go, especially if it's on sale.

Overall the game was enjoyable and I liked getting to read through all of the documents and web pages. The story was also interesting. If you like narrative-heavy games, you'll probably enjoy this. 

Now, what I didn't like:

- Some of the information I submitted was counted as 'not relevant', but it feels unrealistic that this information wouldn't be relevant. For example, finding out that two characters who might be collaborating used to be a couple and have since broken up. I would say that's pretty important! I did enjoy some of this mechanic, such as characters obviously being sarcastic with each other, so you don't just add every bit of information you see.

- There's no hint button so if you get stuck, you have to resort to looking at a walkthrough.

- There's no way to skip through phone calls or text conversations and just read the transcript at the end. The final chapter has a verrrrry long phone call with an ending-deciding choice afterwards, and if you want to replay the final day and unlock the other endings you have to sit through the whole thing again. If these calls were voice acted I wouldn't mind, but you're just watching text appear onscreen at its own pace for what feels like forever.

For example, finding out that two characters who might be collaborating used to be a couple and have since broken up. I would say that's pretty important! I did enjoy some of this mechanic, such as characters obviously being sarcastic with each other, so you don't just add every bit of information you see. - There's no hint button so if you get stuck, you have to resort to looking at a walkthrough. - There's no way to skip through phone calls or text conversations and just read the transcript at the end. The final chapter has a verrrrry long phone call with an ending-deciding choice afterwards, and if you want to replay the final day and unlock the other endings you have to sit through the whole thing again. If these calls were voice acted I wouldn't mind, but you're just watching text appear onscreen at its own pace for what feels like forever.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Short, but Sweet. (*Mild spoilers, but not in detail or specific*)

Good game - very intense, with an aquired taste in art/aesthetic that I personally enjoyed. It was quite philosophical. Also, unlike many of it's competing "episodic" games (looking at you Telltale), the choices you make genuinely affect the gameplay, as well as the endings (and yes, I did finish the job... like my playthrough of LiS, why wouldn't I continue the very thing I had done the entire game?). The gameplay is detailed and intelligent.

My biggest issue is, as with many episodic games, the short timespan. The game is very short - and this also includes periods of time where you can't do anything, such as during the phone call and text sections. Also, there isn't too much of a progression system - for example, one of the better mechanics called "Insider" is only given to you near the climax of the game's story, and it is only used for about a tenth of the game's span. 

All in all, I do thoroughly recommend the game, especially if you want an intense yet oddly chilled experience (think of it as like a UAV flying simulator, except more personal) as well as ethical thinking as a genuinely thought provoking insight to the current age of omnipresent technology. However, if you want something that you can keep playing (for example, endgame content, replay value etc), then it probably isn't for you.

Overall great writing, interesting characters, nice visual interface, and replayability to see how different choices affect the game's outcome.

review_text_raw:
Fun game.  A very unique experience. Browsing through blogs, Orwell's version of facebook or tapping into someone's phone call, you slowly build up a big web of profiles for potential suspects in an attempt to prevent people from getting hurt.  
However, it feels a bit restrictive at times.  It's not like the real internet where you can go wherever you want and freely look up things.  New websites gradually unlock for you to browse only when you get more clues.  Eg: go to this website, find the keywords that will open up more sites for you to browse, then find more keywords.  To be fair, it would be very difficult to make a game as open as the real internet.
All in all though, it was fun and I recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Interesting game with a cool, if a bit heavy-handed, social commentary narrative. The game consists of you sifting through text conversations, articles and phone call transcripts to connect the dots and stop a terror plot.

While the reporting system is selective about what you can include in reports, it is also pretty dumb so some stuff is best left out, making the game more engaging than just "click the thing". You also need to make some decisions in real time that will impact how the story unfolds. I love the mechanic of asynchronous information between you and your suppervisor.

Overall: if you like story-oriented games and want something new and interesting, this game is worth around 10-15 bucks.
